prompt: Which statement expresses Hess's law?

choices.text: When chemical equations are combined algebraically, their ΔH values are combined in the same way.
When chemical equations are added, the overall ΔH is the largest of their ΔH values.
choices.why: The ΔH values are combined just as the equations are, so adding equations means adding all of their ΔH values, not picking the largest one.

choices.text: When chemical equations are added, their ΔH values are multiplied together.
choices.why: Adding equations means adding their ΔH values. Multiplying applies only when one equation is multiplied by a number, and then its ΔH is multiplied by that same number.

choices.text: The ΔH of a reaction can be found only by carrying out that reaction in a calorimeter.
choices.why: Hess's law is what lets us calculate the ΔH of a reaction from other reactions, without measuring it directly.

explanation: Hess's law states that when chemical equations are combined algebraically, their enthalpies can be combined in exactly the same way. When equations are added, their ΔH values are added.

prompt: A thermochemical equation is written in reverse, so its products become reactants and its reactants become products. What happens to its ΔH?

choices.text: It keeps the same size but changes sign.
It stays the same, since the same substances are involved.
choices.why: Reversing a reaction reverses its energy change: a reaction that gives off energy absorbs the same amount when it runs backward, so the sign of ΔH changes.

choices.text: It changes sign only if the original reaction was exothermic.
choices.why: The rule applies to every reaction. Reversing an endothermic reaction also changes the sign, so the reverse reaction is exothermic.

choices.text: It becomes its reciprocal, 1/ΔH.
choices.why: ΔH is not inverted. The reverse reaction involves the same amount of energy, so only the sign of ΔH changes.

explanation: The first corollary of Hess's law: if a chemical reaction is reversed, the sign on ΔH is changed. The size stays the same, so an exothermic reaction becomes an equally large endothermic one.

prompt: In Hess's law, chemical equations are treated like algebraic equations, with the arrow acting like an equals sign. How are two chemical equations added?

choices.text: All the reactants of both equations go to the left of the arrow, and all the products of both go to the right.
Only the reactants of the first equation and the products of the second equation are kept.
choices.why: Nothing is dropped when equations are added. Every reactant and product is kept until substances that appear on both sides are canceled.

choices.text: The coefficients of a substance found in both equations are multiplied together.
choices.why: When the same substance appears on the same side of both equations, its amounts are added, not multiplied.

choices.text: The reactants of the second equation are written on the product side of the first.
choices.why: Each substance stays on the side of the arrow it started on: reactants are combined with reactants, and products with products.

explanation: Like algebraic equations, chemical equations are added by combining all the reactants together and all the products together. Any substance that then appears on both sides of the arrow can be canceled.

prompt: After two chemical equations are added, 2SO2(g) appears on both the reactant side and the product side of the arrow. What should be done with it?

choices.text: Cancel it from both sides, much like a spectator ion.
Keep it on both sides, since it came from both equations.
choices.why: A substance with the same amount on both sides of the arrow is not changed overall, so it is canceled.

choices.text: Move it all to the reactant side as 4SO2(g).
choices.why: Amounts on opposite sides of the arrow are subtracted, not added; equal amounts on both sides cancel completely.

choices.text: Cancel it from the product side only.
choices.why: Canceling removes the same amount from both sides of the arrow, just as you subtract the same quantity from both sides of an algebraic equation.

explanation: If the same substance appears on both sides of the arrow, it can be canceled out, much like a spectator ion in an ionic equation. Here all of the 2SO2(g) cancels from both sides.

prompt: Why is Hess's law so useful to chemists?

choices.text: It gives the ΔH of a hard-to-perform reaction by combining equations whose ΔH values are known.
It makes a hard-to-perform reaction take place once its equation is written as a sum of others.
choices.why: Writing an equation as a sum of other equations is done on paper. It lets you calculate ΔH, but it does not make the reaction happen.

choices.text: It turns an endothermic reaction into an exothermic one when its equation is reversed.
choices.why: Reversing an equation describes the reverse reaction; it does not change the energy change of the original reaction.

choices.text: It shows that ΔH stays the same no matter how much of each substance reacts.
choices.why: The amounts matter: when an equation is multiplied by a number, its ΔH is multiplied by the same number.

explanation: Hess's law lets us combine equations to generate new reactions whose enthalpy changes can be calculated rather than directly measured. That is how the ΔH of a reaction that is difficult to perform, such as burning carbon to only CO, can be found.

prompt: Carbon can be burned to carbon dioxide in two ways. Route A: 2C(s) + 2O2(g) → 2CO2(g). Route B: first 2C(s) + O2(g) → 2CO(g), then 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g). How does the total ΔH of route B compare with the ΔH of route A?

choices.text: They are equal, because the two steps of route B add up to the equation for route A.
Route B gives off more energy in total, because it has two exothermic steps instead of one.
choices.why: Adding route B's steps and canceling 2CO(g) gives exactly the route A equation, so by Hess's law their ΔH values add up to route A's ΔH. The number of steps doesn't matter.

choices.text: Route B gives off less energy in total, because some energy is lost in making CO along the way.
choices.why: No energy is lost between steps: the ΔH of making CO plus the ΔH of burning that CO equals the ΔH of burning carbon directly to CO2.

choices.text: They can't be compared without measuring both routes in a calorimeter.
choices.why: Hess's law lets you compare them without measuring: route B's steps combine algebraically into route A, so their ΔH values combine the same way.

explanation: Adding route B's equations gives 2C(s) + 2O2(g) + 2CO(g) → 2CO(g) + 2CO2(g), and canceling 2CO(g) leaves the route A equation. By Hess's law the ΔH values combine the same way, so both routes have the same total ΔH.

prompt: Add these two equations and cancel everything that can be canceled: (1) 4Cu(s) + 2O2(g) → 4CuO(s); (2) 4CuO(s) → 2Cu2O(s) + O2(g). What is the overall equation?

choices.text: 4Cu(s) + O2(g) → 2Cu2O(s)
4Cu(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Cu2O(s)
choices.why: The O2(g) on the product side cancels 1 mol of the O2(g) on the reactant side; it is subtracted, not added.
O2(g) still appears on both sides, so 1 mol of it can be canceled from each side.

choices.text: 4Cu(s) + 2O2(g) → 2Cu2O(s)
choices.why: Canceling takes the same amount off both sides: removing 1 mol of O2(g) from the products also removes 1 mol from the reactants. This equation isn't even balanced.

explanation: Combining gives 4Cu(s) + 2O2(g) + 4CuO(s) → 4CuO(s) + 2Cu2O(s) + O2(g). All of the 4CuO(s) cancels, and 1 mol of O2(g) cancels from each side, leaving 4Cu(s) + O2(g) → 2Cu2O(s).

prompt: To find ΔH for CS2(ℓ) + 3O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2SO2(g), you are given (1) C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; (2) S(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), ΔH = −296.8 kJ; (3) C(s) + 2S(s) → CS2(ℓ), ΔH = +89.7 kJ. CS2 appears only in equation 3. How should equation 3 be used?

choices.text: Reverse it, so CS2(ℓ) is a reactant and ΔH = −89.7 kJ.
Use it as written, so CS2(ℓ) is a product and ΔH = +89.7 kJ.
choices.why: The target has CS2(ℓ) as a reactant, but equation 3 has it as a product, so equation 3 must be reversed.

choices.text: Reverse it, so CS2(ℓ) is a reactant and ΔH = +89.7 kJ.
choices.why: Reversing a reaction changes the sign of its ΔH, so +89.7 kJ becomes −89.7 kJ.

choices.text: Multiply it by 2, so 2CS2(ℓ) forms and ΔH = +179.4 kJ.
choices.why: The target has 1 mol of CS2(ℓ), the same as equation 3. The 2SO2(g) is matched by doubling equation 2, not equation 3.

explanation: Start with a substance that appears in only one given equation. The target needs 1 mol of CS2(ℓ) as a reactant, so equation 3 is reversed and its ΔH changes sign to −89.7 kJ; adding it to equation 1 and twice equation 2 gives the target.

prompt: To find ΔH for 4Fe(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s), a student uses (1) 2Fe(s) + O2(g) → 2FeO(s), ΔH = −544.0 kJ; (2) 4FeO(s) + O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s), ΔH = −560.4 kJ. What must be done to equation 1 so that FeO(s) cancels?

choices.text: Multiply it by 2, making its ΔH −1,088.0 kJ.
Reverse it, making its ΔH +544.0 kJ.
choices.why: Reversing would put FeO(s) on the reactant side, the same side as in equation 2, so it could not cancel.

choices.text: Multiply it by 2, leaving its ΔH at −544.0 kJ.
choices.why: When an equation is multiplied by a number, its ΔH must be multiplied by the same number.

choices.text: Reverse it and multiply it by 2, making its ΔH +1,088.0 kJ.
choices.why: FeO(s) is already a product in equation 1 and a reactant in equation 2, so equation 1 should not be reversed; it only needs to be doubled.

explanation: Equation 2 uses 4FeO(s) as a reactant, but equation 1 makes only 2FeO(s). Doubling equation 1 gives 4Fe(s) + 2O2(g) → 4FeO(s) with ΔH = 2 × (−544.0 kJ) = −1,088.0 kJ, and then the 4FeO(s) cancels.

prompt: To find ΔH for 2H2O2(ℓ) → 2H2O(ℓ) + O2(g), you are given (1) H2(g) + O2(g) → H2O2(ℓ), ΔH = −187.8 kJ; (2) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −571.6 kJ. How must equation 1 be changed before the equations are added?

choices.text: Reverse it and multiply it by 2, making its ΔH +375.6 kJ.
Reverse it only, making its ΔH +187.8 kJ.
choices.why: The target has 2 mol of H2O2(ℓ), so after reversing, the equation and its ΔH must also be doubled.

choices.text: Multiply it by 2 only, making its ΔH −375.6 kJ.
choices.why: H2O2(ℓ) is a product in equation 1 but a reactant in the target, so the equation must also be reversed, which changes the sign of ΔH.

choices.text: Reverse it and multiply it by 2, making its ΔH −375.6 kJ.
choices.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH, so −187.8 kJ becomes +187.8 kJ, and doubling gives +375.6 kJ.

explanation: The target has 2H2O2(ℓ) as a reactant, so equation 1 is reversed (ΔH = +187.8 kJ) and doubled (ΔH = +375.6 kJ). Adding equation 2 then cancels 2H2(g) and 1 mol of O2(g), giving ΔH = +375.6 + (−571.6) = −196.0 kJ for the target.

prompt: A student wants ΔH for N2(g) + 2O2(g) → 2NO2(g) from (1) N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180.5 kJ; (2) 2NO2(g) → 2NO(g) + O2(g), ΔH = +114.1 kJ. The student rewrites equation 2 as 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g), ΔH = +114.1 kJ, adds it to equation 1, and reports ΔH = +294.6 kJ. What went wrong?

choices.text: Equation 2 was reversed, but the sign of its ΔH was not changed.
Equation 2 should not have been reversed.
choices.why: NO2(g) is a product in the target but a reactant in equation 2, so reversing equation 2 was the right move.

choices.text: Equation 1 should have been reversed as well.
choices.why: Equation 1 already has N2(g) as a reactant, as the target does, so it is used as written.

choices.text: Equation 2 should also have been multiplied by 2.
choices.why: Equation 2 already contains 2NO2(g), the amount in the target, so it doesn't need to be multiplied.

explanation: Reversing equation 2 is correct, but its ΔH must then change sign to −114.1 kJ. The correct result is ΔH = +180.5 + (−114.1) = +66.4 kJ.

prompt: In a blast furnace, carbon monoxide reduces iron ore. A student wants ΔH for 2Fe2O3(s) + 6CO(g) → 4Fe(s) + 6CO2(g) from (1) 4Fe(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s), ΔH = −1,648.4 kJ; (2) 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH = −566.0 kJ. The student reports ΔH = +1,082.4 kJ. Which single mistake explains this answer?

choices.text: The ΔH of equation 2 was not multiplied by 3.
The sign of equation 1's ΔH was not changed when it was reversed.
Equation 2 was reversed when it should have been used as written.
The ΔH values of both equations were multiplied by 3.

explanation: The correct steps are to reverse equation 1 (ΔH = +1,648.4 kJ) and multiply equation 2 by 3 (ΔH = −1,698.0 kJ), giving ΔH = −49.6 kJ. Using −566.0 kJ only once instead gives +1,648.4 + (−566.0) = +1,082.4 kJ.

prompt: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose: C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −2,803 kJ. Photosynthesis runs this overall reaction in reverse. What is ΔH for 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(ℓ) → C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: The photosynthesis equation is the respiration equation reversed, so its ΔH has the same size and the opposite sign: +2,803 kJ.

prompt: The Haber process makes ammonia: N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92.2 kJ. What is ΔH for 3N2(g) + 9H2(g) → 6NH3(g)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: The new equation is the original multiplied by 3, so its ΔH is multiplied by 3 as well: 3 × (−92.2 kJ) = −276.6 kJ.

prompt: Methane can be made from its elements: C(s) + 2H2(g) → CH4(g), ΔH = −74.8 kJ. Methane pyrolysis does the opposite, splitting methane into solid carbon and hydrogen gas without making any CO2. What is ΔH for 3CH4(g) → 3C(s) + 6H2(g)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: The pyrolysis equation is the given equation reversed and multiplied by 3. Reversing changes ΔH to +74.8 kJ, and tripling gives ΔH = 3 × (+74.8 kJ) = +224.4 kJ.

prompt: In the old lead-chamber process for making sulfuric acid, nitrogen dioxide oxidizes sulfur dioxide: 2SO2(g) + 2NO2(g) → 2SO3(g) + 2NO(g). Find ΔH for this reaction from (1) 2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g), ΔH = −197.8 kJ; (2) 2NO(g) + O2(g) → 2NO2(g), ΔH = −114.1 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written and reverse equation 2 (ΔH = +114.1 kJ) so that NO2(g) is a reactant; the O2(g) then cancels. ΔH = −197.8 + 114.1 = −83.7 kJ.

prompt: The thermite reaction, used to weld railroad rails, is 2Al(s) + Fe2O3(s) → Al2O3(s) + 2Fe(s). Find its ΔH from (1) 4Al(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Al2O3(s), ΔH = −3,351.4 kJ; (2) 4Fe(s) + 3O2(g) → 2Fe2O3(s), ΔH = −1,648.4 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Take half of equation 1 (ΔH = −1,675.7 kJ) and half of equation 2, reversed (ΔH = +824.2 kJ); the 3/2 O2(g) cancels. ΔH = −1,675.7 + 824.2 = −851.5 kJ.

prompt: When wine turns to vinegar, ethanol is oxidized to acetic acid: C2H5OH(ℓ) + O2(g) → CH3COOH(ℓ) + H2O(ℓ). Find ΔH for this reaction from the combustion reactions (1) C2H5OH(ℓ) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −1,367 kJ; (2) CH3COOH(ℓ) + 2O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −874 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written and reverse equation 2 (ΔH = +874 kJ). On adding, 2CO2(g) cancels, and 2O2(g) and 2H2O(ℓ) cancel from each side, leaving the target with ΔH = −1,367 + 874 = −493 kJ.

prompt: Turning graphite into diamond takes enormous pressure, so its ΔH is found from combustion data instead: (1) C(s, graphite) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; (2) C(s, diamond) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = −395.4 kJ. What is ΔH for C(s, graphite) → C(s, diamond)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written and reverse equation 2 (ΔH = +395.4 kJ); O2(g) and CO2(g) cancel. ΔH = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ.

prompt: Hydrazine and dinitrogen tetroxide ignite on contact and have been used together as rocket propellants: 2N2H4(ℓ) + N2O4(g) → 3N2(g) + 4H2O(ℓ). Find ΔH for this reaction from (1) N2H4(ℓ) + O2(g) → N2(g) + 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −622.2 kJ; (2) N2(g) + 2O2(g) → N2O4(g), ΔH = +9.1 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Double equation 1 (ΔH = −1,244.4 kJ) and reverse equation 2 (ΔH = −9.1 kJ); 2O2(g) cancels, and the N2(g) adds up to 3N2(g). ΔH = −1,244.4 + (−9.1) = −1,253.5 kJ.

prompt: The Deacon process makes chlorine from hydrogen chloride: 4HCl(g) + O2(g) → 2Cl2(g) + 2H2O(g). Find its ΔH from (1) H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g), ΔH = −184.6 kJ; (2) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g), ΔH = −483.6 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Reverse equation 1 and multiply it by 2 (ΔH = +369.2 kJ) so that 4HCl(g) is a reactant, then add equation 2; 2H2(g) cancels. ΔH = +369.2 + (−483.6) = −114.4 kJ.

prompt: Lime mortar hardens as slaked lime absorbs carbon dioxide from the air: Ca(OH)2(s) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s) + H2O(ℓ). Find ΔH for this reaction from (1) CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), ΔH = +178.3 kJ; (2) CaO(s) + H2O(ℓ) → Ca(OH)2(s), ΔH = −65.2 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Both equations must be reversed: CaO(s) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s), ΔH = −178.3 kJ, and Ca(OH)2(s) → CaO(s) + H2O(ℓ), ΔH = +65.2 kJ. CaO(s) cancels, and ΔH = −178.3 + 65.2 = −113.1 kJ.

prompt: High in the atmosphere, oxygen atoms destroy ozone: 2O3(g) + 2O(g) → 4O2(g). Find ΔH for this reaction from (1) 2O3(g) → 3O2(g), ΔH = −285 kJ; (2) O2(g) → 2O(g), ΔH = +498 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written and reverse equation 2 (ΔH = −498 kJ) so that 2O(g) is a reactant. The O2(g) adds up to 4O2(g) on the product side, and ΔH = −285 + (−498) = −783 kJ.

prompt: Yeast ferments glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide: C6H12O6(s) → 2C2H5OH(ℓ) + 2CO2(g). Find ΔH for this reaction from the combustion reactions (1) C6H12O6(s) + 6O2(g) → 6CO2(g) + 6H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −2,803 kJ; (2) C2H5OH(ℓ) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −1,367 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written, and reverse equation 2 and multiply it by 2 (ΔH = +2,734 kJ). 6O2(g) and 6H2O(ℓ) cancel, and 4CO2(g) cancels from each side, leaving 2CO2(g) as a product; ΔH = −2,803 + 2,734 = −69 kJ.

prompt: Sulfuric acid is made from sulfur in three steps: (1) S(s) + O2(g) → SO2(g), ΔH = −296.8 kJ; (2) 2SO2(g) + O2(g) → 2SO3(g), ΔH = −197.8 kJ; (3) SO3(g) + H2O(ℓ) → H2SO4(ℓ), ΔH = −132.5 kJ. What is ΔH for the overall reaction 2S(s) + 3O2(g) + 2H2O(ℓ) → 2H2SO4(ℓ)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Multiply equation 1 by 2 (−593.6 kJ), use equation 2 as written (−197.8 kJ), and multiply equation 3 by 2 (−265.0 kJ); 2SO2(g) and 2SO3(g) cancel. ΔH = −593.6 − 197.8 − 265.0 = −1,056.4 kJ.

prompt: Methanol is made industrially from carbon monoxide and hydrogen: 2CO(g) + 4H2(g) → 2CH3OH(ℓ). Find ΔH for this reaction from (1) 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH = −566.0 kJ; (2) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −571.6 kJ; (3) 2CH3OH(ℓ) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 4H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −1,452.8 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Use equation 1 as written, multiply equation 2 by 2 (−1,143.2 kJ), and reverse equation 3 (+1,452.8 kJ); 2CO2(g), 3O2(g), and 4H2O(ℓ) cancel. ΔH = −566.0 − 1,143.2 + 1,452.8 = −256.4 kJ.

prompt: The ΔH for making propane from its elements, 3C(s) + 4H2(g) → C3H8(g), can't be measured directly, but it can be found from combustion data: (1) C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; (2) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −571.6 kJ; (3) C3H8(g) + 5O2(g) → 3CO2(g) + 4H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −2,219.9 kJ. What is ΔH for making propane from its elements? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Multiply equation 1 by 3 (−1,180.5 kJ), multiply equation 2 by 2 (−1,143.2 kJ), and reverse equation 3 (+2,219.9 kJ); 3CO2(g), 5O2(g), and 4H2O(ℓ) cancel. ΔH = −1,180.5 − 1,143.2 + 2,219.9 = −103.8 kJ.

prompt: The first step in making nitric acid is burning ammonia: 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g). Find its ΔH from (1) N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), ΔH = −92.2 kJ; (2) N2(g) + O2(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180.5 kJ; (3) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g), ΔH = −483.6 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Reverse equation 1 and multiply it by 2 (+184.4 kJ), multiply equation 2 by 2 (+361.0 kJ), and multiply equation 3 by 3 (−1,450.8 kJ); 2N2(g) and 6H2(g) cancel. ΔH = +184.4 + 361.0 − 1,450.8 = −905.4 kJ.

prompt: Most hydrogen gas is made by steam reforming of methane: 2CH4(g) + 2H2O(g) → 2CO(g) + 6H2(g). Find its ΔH from (1) CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH = −802.3 kJ; (2) 2CO(g) + O2(g) → 2CO2(g), ΔH = −566.0 kJ; (3) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g), ΔH = −483.6 kJ. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Multiply equation 1 by 2 (−1,604.6 kJ), reverse equation 2 (+566.0 kJ), and reverse equation 3 and multiply it by 3 (+1,450.8 kJ). 2CO2(g) and 4O2(g) cancel, and 4H2O(g) cancels from each side, leaving 2H2O(g) as a reactant; ΔH = −1,604.6 + 566.0 + 1,450.8 = +412.2 kJ.

prompt: Burning magnesium gives an intensely hot, bright flame that is hard to study in a coffee-cup calorimeter, so students measure two gentler reactions instead and add a third, known one: (1) Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g), ΔH = −466.8 kJ; (2) MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −151.0 kJ; (3) 2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(ℓ), ΔH = −571.6 kJ. What is ΔH for 2Mg(s) + O2(g) → 2MgO(s)? Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Multiply equation 1 by 2 (−933.6 kJ), reverse equation 2 and multiply it by 2 (+302.0 kJ), and use equation 3 as written; 4HCl(aq), 2MgCl2(aq), 2H2(g), and 2H2O(ℓ) cancel. ΔH = −933.6 + 302.0 − 571.6 = −1,203.2 kJ.
